summary: Describes addressing and routing strategies for enterprises connected to multiple Internet service providers, intended to reduce the load such enterprises place on the global routing system. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: If a company has two internet providers, routers worldwide have to remember extra things. This shows ways to keep that load smaller.

questions: how to multihome with multiple isps
how does multihoming affect internet routing
how to multihome without growing the internet routing table
subtitle: How a network with several ISPs can stay reachable without bloating the Internet's core routing tables.

tldr.problem: Enterprises connect to more than one ISP for reliability and load sharing, but a separate route for each one in the default-free zone of the Internet does not scale.
tldr.mechanism: Each ISP allocates the enterprise its own prefix, and the enterprise normally advertises only that ISP's prefix to it. When another ISP link fails, it advertises the other prefix too (auto route injection), or uses non-direct EBGP peering with encapsulation so no extra routes are needed.
tldr.outcome: The routing overhead in the default-free zone is greatly reduced, or with non-direct EBGP removed, at the cost of renumbering when changing ISPs and careful address assignment. It is an Informational memo.

today: RFC 2260 is an Informational memo from January 1998 and is not obsoleted or updated by any other RFC. It does not specify an Internet standard of any kind.

sections.title: Why Multi-homing Strains Routing
sections.content:
An enterprise may buy connectivity from more than one ISP to make its Internet access more reliable, to spread load over several connections, or to get better routing when it covers a wide geographic area. Falling prices push more enterprises to do this.

The memo assumes that requiring every router in the default-free zone to carry a route for each such enterprise does not scale. It also assumes that any approach should need as little coordination as possible among ISPs, especially ISPs not directly connected to the enterprise. The strategies apply equally to IPv4 and IPv6. Whether multi-homing to a single ISP could meet the same needs is declared out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: More and more companies want two mail carriers in case one is sick. But if every post office in the world had to write down both carriers for every company, their notebooks would overflow.

sections.title: Address Allocation and Assignment
sections.content:
An enterprise connected to N ISPs gets N different address blocks, one from each ISP, under the address-lending policy of RFC 2008. These addresses are then used inside the enterprise.

One possible plan is to pick a host's prefix by how close the host is topologically to a particular ISP connection. A host may be given addresses from one prefix or from several.
sections.plainLanguage: Each carrier gives the company its own set of street numbers. Inside the company, each room uses the numbers from whichever carrier's door is nearest.

sections.title: Auto Route Injection
sections.content:
While the enterprise is connected to the Internet through all of its ISPs, each enterprise border router advertises to its ISP only the prefix that ISP allocated. The ISP aggregates it, so it does not reach the default-free zone.

When a border router decides that connectivity through another ISP is down, it also starts advertising that ISP's prefix. This adds routes to the default-free zone, but the memo argues that on average only a small fraction of multi-homed enterprises will have such a failure at once.

The memo gives BGP (RFC 1771) as one way to detect failure: border routers run IBGP with each other, and a border router starts injecting when the intersection between the routes it hears over EBGP and the routes it hears over IBGP is empty. This is called auto route injection. As a cheaper alternative, a router can watch one well-known prefix, such as the other ISP's backbone route, and inject when it is withdrawn.

A caveat: ISPs that filter routes by prefix length may leave the enterprise with less than full connectivity, which the memo says would be a problem however the enterprise set up its routing.
sections.plainLanguage: Normally the company only tells each carrier about that carrier's own street numbers. If one carrier's road washes out, the other carrier is told to also deliver for the missing numbers.

sections.title: Non-direct EBGP and Combining the Approaches
sections.content:
To remove the overhead entirely, an enterprise border router also keeps an EBGP session with an ISP border router that is connected to a different enterprise border router. This is non-direct EBGP. The ISP advertises the same routes over direct and non-direct sessions, and the enterprise advertises the prefix that ISP allocated over either. Routes learned over direct peering are preferred, both inside the ISP and inside the enterprise.

When the link between ISP-B's border router and the enterprise fails, traffic for the Pref-B addresses still arrives at ISP-B's border router, which encapsulates it (RFC 1773) and sends it to the enterprise's other border router. That router decapsulates it and delivers it inside. No extra routes enter the default-free zone, and the scheme does not suffer from ISPs filtering by prefix length. Non-direct peering may be with any router in the ISP, which can improve robustness.

Non-direct EBGP can give suboptimal routing when links fail. The memo suggests combining it with auto route injection, limiting how far the injected routes spread using the BGP Community attribute (RFC 1997). The same attribute can constrain optional steady-state advertisements of other ISPs' prefixes that give better paths.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of telling the whole world, the company arranges a secret side door. If one carrier's road is closed, that carrier wraps the packages in a bigger package and sends them to the company's other door.

sections.title: Comparison and Trade-offs
sections.content:
The memo compares its approach with two options from RFC 1518. In the first, the enterprise gets its own address space independent of any ISP. This cannot be aggregated, so the load in the default-free zone is O(N), where N is the number of multi-homed enterprises, which the memo says is not viable for most of them. In the second, the enterprise takes a prefix from one ISP and the other ISPs do careful 'proxy' aggregation, which needs more inter-ISP coordination and more complex configuration.

The memo's own approach means the enterprise must renumber part of its network when it changes ISPs, but it points out that single-homed enterprises face the same, and it needs careful address assignment because that affects traffic distribution. Auto route injection exposes more default-free routers to changes than provider-independent addresses would. To limit flapping, the injected route has to stay advertised until the other connection is stable. Non-direct EBGP removes flapping from the default-free zone altogether.

A small to medium ISP with several upstream ISPs can use the same techniques toward its upstreams.
sections.plainLanguage: The other ways either make everyone remember too much or need all the post offices to chat constantly. This way costs the company a bit of address changing when it switches carriers.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: Non-direct EBGP needs EBGP sessions between routers that are more than one IP hop apart. The memo says those routers should use an appropriate BGP peer authentication mechanism. Security of IBGP and of EBGP between routers one hop apart is out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: If a side door lets packages in from far away, the guards at that door should check who is knocking.
